summary.text: Counting pairs divisible by each power of \(p\) in the gcd product and using the factorial valuation formula for the denominator gives \(v_p(a(m))=\sum_{i\ge1} g(\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor)\), where \(g(t)=\sum_{r=1}^t(t\bmod r)\). For \(0\le k<p\), every quotient \(\lfloor(np+k)/p^i\rfloor\) with \(i\ge1\) equals \(\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\), so the valuation sums are identical.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(m)=\prod_{j=1}^m\prod_{r=1}^m \gcd(j,r),
\qquad
D(m)=\prod_{q=1}^m\left(\left\lfloor\frac mq\right\rfloor !\right)^q.
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N(m)}{D(m)}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and derive a formula for its valuation at an arbitrary prime.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). We use the elementary facts
\[
v_p(xy)=v_p(x)+v_p(y),\qquad
v_p(x^q)=qv_p(x),
\]
\[
v_p(\gcd(x,y))=\min(v_p(x),v_p(y)),
\]
and Legendre’s formula
\[
v_p(t!)=\sum_{i\ge 1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
All sums over \(i\) occurring below are actually finite, since their terms vanish once \(p^i\) exceeds the relevant integer.

We begin with the numerator. By additivity of valuations over products and the valuation formula for a gcd,
\[
v_p(N(m))
 =\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{r=1}^m
   \min(v_p(j),v_p(r)).
\]
For any two positive integers \(j,r\),
\[
\min(v_p(j),v_p(r))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}{\bf 1}_{p^i\mid j}\,{\bf 1}_{p^i\mid r}.
\]
Indeed, the summand is one precisely for those positive \(i\) not exceeding both \(v_p(j)\) and \(v_p(r)\), and the number of such \(i\) is their minimum. Interchanging the finite sums gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(N(m))
 &=\sum_{i\ge1}
   \left(\sum_{j=1}^m {\bf 1}_{p^i\mid j}\right)
   \left(\sum_{r=1}^m {\bf 1}_{p^i\mid r}\right)\\
 &=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
because exactly \(\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\) integers in \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) are divisible by \(p^i\). It is convenient, and harmless, to truncate this at \(i=m\):
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
v_p(N(m))=\sum_{i=1}^m\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2.}
\tag{1}
\]
For \(m=0\) both sides are empty sums. For \(m>0\), a prime satisfies \(p\ge2\), so \(p^i>m\) for all sufficiently large \(i\), and in particular every omitted term after any sufficiently large bound is zero; the bound \(m\) is more than enough.

Next consider the denominator. Applying the product and power rules and then Legendre’s formula,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(D(m))
 &=\sum_{q=1}^m q\,
   v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac mq\right\rfloor!\right)\\
 &=\sum_{q=1}^m q\sum_{i\ge1}
   \left\lfloor
   \frac{\lfloor m/q\rfloor}{p^i}
   \right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
The elementary nested-floor identity for positive divisors gives
\[
\left\lfloor
\frac{\lfloor m/q\rfloor}{p^i}
\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q p^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor
\frac{\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor}{q}
\right\rfloor.
\]
After interchanging the finite sums, set
\[
t_i=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(q>t_i\), then \(\lfloor t_i/q\rfloor=0\), so the sum over \(q\) may be restricted to \(1\le q\le t_i\). Again truncating the outer sum at \(m\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
v_p(D(m))
=\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{q=1}^{t_i}
q\left\lfloor\frac{t_i}{q}\right\rfloor,
\qquad t_i=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor.}
\tag{2}
\]

We now show that \(D(m)\) really divides \(N(m)\). For every nonnegative integer \(t\) and every \(1\le q\le t\),
\[
q\left\lfloor\frac tq\right\rfloor\le t.
\]
There are \(t\) values of \(q\) in the sum, and hence
\[
\sum_{q=1}^t q\left\lfloor\frac tq\right\rfloor\le t^2.
\tag{3}
\]
Comparing (1) and (2) term by term by means of (3) shows that, for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p(D(m))\le v_p(N(m)).
\]
Both \(D(m)\) and \(N(m)\) are positive: factorials are positive, and every gcd in the numerator is positive because its arguments range from \(1\) to \(m\). The prime-factorization criterion for divisibility therefore yields
\[
D(m)\mid N(m).
\]
Thus \(a(m)=N(m)/D(m)\) is an exact integer quotient, and
\[
v_p(a(m))=v_p(N(m))-v_p(D(m)).
\tag{4}
\]

Define, for every nonnegative integer \(t\),
\[
G(t)=\sum_{q=1}^t (t\bmod q),
\]
with \(G(0)=0\). Euclidean division says
\[
t=q\left\lfloor\frac tq\right\rfloor+(t\bmod q).
\]
Summing this identity over \(q=1,\ldots,t\) gives
\[
t^2
=\sum_{q=1}^t q\left\lfloor\frac tq\right\rfloor
 +\sum_{q=1}^t(t\bmod q),
\]
and therefore
\[
G(t)=t^2-
\sum_{q=1}^t q\left\lfloor\frac tq\right\rfloor.
\tag{5}
\]
The subtraction is legitimate in the ordinary integers, and (3) also shows directly that the right-hand side is nonnegative.

Substituting (1) and (2) into (4), grouping terms with the same \(i\), and applying (5) to \(t_i=\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\), we arrive at the key formula
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
v_p(a(m))
=\sum_{i=1}^m
G\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right).}
\tag{6}
\]

We now prove the required constancy. Let \(n\) be positive, let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy \(0\le k<p\). Put
\[
m_0=np,
\qquad
m_k=np+k.
\]
For every \(i\ge1\), we claim
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{7}
\]
To see this, first divide by \(p\). Since \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n
=
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
For \(i\ge1\), division by \(p^i=p\,p^{i-1}\) can be performed by first taking the quotient upon division by \(p\), and then dividing that quotient by \(p^{i-1}\). Consequently both sides of (7) equal
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor.
\]
This proves (7).

Apply (6) first with \(m=m_0=np\), and then with \(m=m_k=np+k\). For every index \(1\le i\le m_0\), equation (7) makes the corresponding summands equal:
\[
G\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right)
=
G\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m_k}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right).
\tag{8}
\]
It remains only to account for the possibly additional indices
\[
m_0<i\le m_k
\]
in the second sum. A prime is at least \(2\), and for every positive \(i\) one has \(p^i>i\) (for example, this follows from \(p^i\ge2^i>i\)). Thus, if \(i>m_0\), then
\[
p^i>i>m_0,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m_0}{p^i}\right\rfloor=0.
\]
Equation (7) then also gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m_k}{p^i}\right\rfloor=0.
\]
Every extra summand in the second sum is therefore \(G(0)=0\). Combining this fact with (8) yields
\[
v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+k)).
\]
Since this holds for every \(k\) with \(0\le k<p\), it follows that
\[
v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+1))=\cdots=v_p(a(np+p-1)).
\]
This is exactly the asserted conjecture.
